Restoring trust: Embattled CDC, HHS officials on their priorities for 2027" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Federal health officials are focused on rebuilding trust with the public and working across the aisle with the fresh Congress.

In a recent development, centers for Disease Control and Prevention Director Erica Schwartz, M.D., and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr., spoke at the Milken Institute’s Future of Health Summit last week in Washington, D.C. Over 1,200 attendees gathered at the event, the theme of which was “better health within reach.”.

In a fireside chat, a chipper Schwartz tried to answer a tough line of questioning about Americans’ loss of trust in her agency, controversial vaccine changes, measles and other public health challenges.

Recent findings suggest that when asked about her potential disagreements with Kennedy, Schwartz said, “I disagree all the time. He’s a lawyer, I’m a lawyer. […] What I love about the secretary is that he listens to those disagreements. He's not someone who just says, ‘No, I don't have room for that.’ He really does value differing opinions.”.

According to recent reports, the U.S. has lost its measles elimination status, global health officials announced just this week. On that matter, Schwartz stressed the importance of supporting CDC’s state partners on awareness, prevention and surveillance efforts.

Sources indicate that “MMR is the number one way to prevent measles,” Schwartz mentioned. Today’s outbreaks “happen in communities that are very close-knit communities … that typically do not and have not vaccinated their children,” she said. Most cases are currently among kids over the age of five and adults, according to Schwartz.

Under Schwartz’s leadership, the CDC changed its method of reporting measles deaths from real-time reporting by state public health departments to death certificate data, which can face multi-month lags. Schwartz is being investigated by Energy & Commerce Committee Democrats who, during a briefing on CDC’s alleged suppression of the total number of national measles deaths on its dashboard, have called her unresponsive and misleading.

“As the crisis worsens, we are concerned that you continue to direct an effort at CDC to downplay the outbreak and artificially reduce the number of measles deaths that CDC reports to the public, concealing the fact that 10 people have died of measles-related deaths this year alone,” the Committee leaders wrote (PDF) in a letter on Tuesday. “We are expanding our investigation to examine the threat your actions pose to Americans’ health and whether changes to your statutory authority are required.”.

It has been revealed that during her fireside chat, Schwartz acknowledged that "we've lost trust not only externally with the American public, but also internally with the team that works at the CDC,” she said. To address this, Schwartz wants the public to understand that CDC follows the science, is being transparent and “leading with humility.” She pointed to COVID-era “arrogance” from institutions, directing at instead of conversing with the public.

“I want to be a CDC director that really has a conversation with the American public,” Schwartz noted.

Internally, the first priority is to add stability to the body, including hiring leaders within the agency so they have a permanent leadership role. The CDC has also created a strategic hiring plan for 2027 with the input of staff and is looking to its “force extenders” like epidemic intelligence officers and its Public Health Associate Program.

On how she’s planning to work with the upcoming majority-Democratic Congress, Schwartz noted she was encouraged to see more Congress members coming in with a healthcare background, “who understand how these policies will impact patients.” She said is eager to work with the Congressional Doctors Caucus and to work with both sides of the aisle.

“I know that we may not agree on every issue, but I do think there's a common ground where we can actually focus on really trying to make Americans healthy again,” she said.

One of her priorities for 2027 is having a “21st-century CDC” by bringing innovation into the public health sphere. She called out the Biothreat Radar, a proposed wastewater surveillance program about which she recently spoke with Sen. Andy Kim (D-New Jersey). The program’s proposed (PDF) budget is $52 million. The CDC has also tentatively put out a call for new Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) members, which will depend on a final ruling from the appellate court in the agency’s favor.

In a recent development, at the Summit, Schwartz’s comments did not necessarily satisfy some of the attendees. When asked by Fierce Healthcare for his impressions of the interview, a public health worker in the room who did not wish to be named called her a “traitor.".

In his fireside chat closing out the Summit, Secretary Kennedy primarily spoke about food and obesity.

One of HHS' most consequential accomplishments during his tenure, Kennedy remarked, has been changing the dietary guidelines to be “science-based.” Earlier this year, the White House released upcoming federal dietary guidelines, calling for prioritizing quality protein, healthy fats, fruits, vegetables and whole grains, while avoiding highly processed foods and refined carbs.

The agency is focused on transforming food across a number of sectors, including in Head Start programs—free federal early childhood programs—which have received about $151 million in supplemental HHS awards to strengthen nutrition services. HHS is also focused on rolling out healthy food options in the military, Kennedy mentioned, and within SNAP by allowing states to request waivers to restrict what SNAP dollars are spent on. As of this summer, HHS has launched a Make Hospital Food Healthier Pledge, challenging hospitals to put nutrition at the center of patient care. HHS has also encouraged medical schools to increase their number of education hours on nutrition from an average of two to 40 hours, Kennedy said.

In a recent development, “Real” food sales in grocery stores, Kennedy claimed, went up 8% this year, while obesity rates have dropped by 7%. He acknowledged that the drop in obesity rates is more likely due to GLP-1 access rather than healthier eating. “If we can reduce obesity, we can reduce our healthcare costs,” he noted, praising Trump’s Most Favored Nation negotiations for lowering the price of drugs like Ozempic.

Industry observers note that “We reward people at every level—the hospitals, the providers, other providers, doctors, insurance companies, pharmaceutical companies—we reward them financially for keeping people sick. And as long as those financial incentives are in place, we are going to be operating a sick-care system rather than a healthcare system,” Kennedy said. HHS has started to change that by shifting more to value-based care, he added, so stakeholders get paid to keep patients healthy “rather than being paid to keep them sick.”.

Recent findings suggest that when asked what he wants his legacy as Health Secretary to be, Kennedy echoed Schwartz on the idea of following science. “What I want to do is to end corporate capture and the politicization of science … that Americans once again trust the regulatory agencies, they trust the science that’s coming from them,” he said.

Industry observers note that he referred to newer guidelines meant to encourage extra transparency from researchers. In 2026, the HHS Scientific Integrity Policy was updated (PDF) to support publishing raw data and code in publicly accessible repositories, preregistering study protocols and transparently reporting all results.

He remarked he wants "to make sure that we’re not kowtowing to the food industry, the pharmaceutical industry, all these people who are at the trough taking on the $2.3 trillion that my agency gives out every year. And that instead, that Americans believe that this agency is devoted to their health, that they trust it, and that we are doing the science that we need to find out what is making them sick so that we can all eliminate it as a society.”.

Kennedy's interview at the event did not touch on measles or vaccine policy, where the secretary's policies and communications have garnered broader criticism and controversy than his views on nutrition. Tuesday's announcement that the U.S. had lost its measles elimination status garnered a fresh call for Kennedy's resignation among his critics, including the Democratic Doctors Caucus.

In a recent development, also coinciding with Milken's event was the announcement of the inaugural 2027 cohort of the Elevate Investment Initiative. The effort, part of the Milken Institute’s Women Health Network, aims to mobilize $1 billion in net-upcoming capital for women’s health innovation. The 10 fund managers and companies include Borski Fund, Cross-Border Impact Ventures, Foreground Capital, Meridian Health Ventures, How Women Invest and more. [cut this or move?].

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A Rosewood Residences branded penthouse has sold for $21 million, setting a record in the elite Los Angeles enclave of Beverly Hills.
  • After only 10 days on the market, Penthouse C at Rosewood Residences Beverly Hills has officially sold for $21 million, discounted from $27.5 million, making it the most expensive developer-sold condominium deal in Beverly Hills this year.
  • At $4,469 per square foot, the transaction ranks as the fifth-highest condominium sale in Los Angeles history by price per square foot.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A Rosewood Residences branded penthouse has sold for $21 million, setting a record in the elite Los Angeles enclave of Beverly Hills.

After only 10 days on the market, Penthouse C at Rosewood Residences Beverly Hills has officially sold for $21 million, discounted from $27.5 million, making it the most expensive developer-sold condominium deal in Beverly Hills this year.

At $4,469 per square foot, the transaction ranks as the fifth-highest condominium sale in Los Angeles history by price per square foot. Only 18 condominiums have ever sold for more than $20 million in the city.

Recent findings suggest that "It was a very quick purchase," sales co-agent Amir Ensani of The Fridman Group at The Beverly Hills Estates tells Realtor.com®. The median days on market is 57, according to Realtor.com data.

Ensani says the buyer, a man in the hospitality industry and his family, was—like all of the buyers in the boutique building—downsizing from a local "megaestate.".

"The massive thing that caught the buyer was a staff of 22 with armed guards," says the luxury broker. Additionally, the buyer, like many other high-net-worth individuals, was migrating to Beverly Hills in part because it has no so-called "mansion tax.".

Enacted in April 2023, the measure imposes a 4% tax on property sales of $5.4 million to $10.9 million, and a 5.5% tax on sales exceeding $10.9 million. These rates apply on top of Los Angeles' standard 0.45% base real estate transfer tax.

Recent findings suggest that the buyer was also a fan of Rosewood Hotels, a global luxury hospitality brand. In Latest York, the tech giant is behind The Carlyle. It does not have a Los Angeles location.

"It's like a double brand," the agent states about living not only inside of the full service Rosewood Residences but the separately incorporated city of Beverly Hills.

Sources indicate that "A lot of the clients are Rosewood connoisseurs, including this one," he says. "They are accustomed to a level of service that Rosewood provides.".

The Rosewood Residences is the only stand-alone residential complex for the brand in the world, a significant plus for the property, claims the broker.

"A lot of people who love the brand may not want a hotel component, with people coming and going," he notes.

Another selling point was that the building is a "pedigree property," built on the site of the former Beverly Hills Friars Club, with interiors designed by Upcoming York-based designer Samuel Amoia.

"He likes to collect pedigree properties," Ensani notes of the buyer. "When he saw it, he was like 'I must have it.'".

The three-bedroom, five-full bathroom penthouse blends sculptural furnishings, collectible art, natural materials, and seamless indoor-outdoor living.

It boasts nearly 4,700 square feet indoors and 2,200 square feet of outdoor space with 25-foot private pool and hot tub, as well as a custom skylit floating staircase, a double-sided fireplace in carved stone, and a private rooftop with a spa and an outdoor kitchen.

The penthouse comes with $18,740 in monthly dues (property taxes not included).

With just 17 residences, the boutique building offers plenty of privacy—the penthouse comes with a private four-car garage—as well as security (the aforementioned armed guards).

The amenity suite includes butler service, personalized fitness training, in-residence spa treatments, house car and driver, valet service, and private chefs.

Next year, the building will welcome two Japanese dining concepts, including a steakhouse and an izakaya (Japanese bar and casual dining).

Recent findings suggest that colisting agent Tomer Fridman notes the units were designed as "estate alternatives" for affluent buyers accustomed to 30,000-square-foot mansions. (Sally Forster Jones of Forster Jones International & Associates at Compass also headed up sales at the complex.).

Industry observers note that "These aren't pieds-à-terre with small galley kitchens," he notes. "They were designed specifically for an audience that is accustomed to huge estates.".

Recent findings suggest that the smallest unit is around 3,200 square feet with around 300 feet of outdoor space, and they top out at 7,200 square feet with 2,400 square feet of outdoor space. Fridman notes it is only one of two condo buildings in Los Angeles with these types of "estate alternative" offerings.

In a recent development, the broker says the generous proportions helped account for the complex's brisk sales, which closed on more more than 50% in presales, a milestone the agency says is unmatched by another LA condominium condo building in the past decade. (The sales team wouldn't say the current percentage of closed sales.).

The estate-like units mean that downsizers can often bring much of their furniture with them—though Penthouse C came fully furnished and curated by the designer himself. Amoia previously designed the architect Robert A.M. Stern building at 520 Park Ave.

Despite the buyers downshifting from sprawling estates, Ensani indicates there is no singular demographic in the building. "We have families, we have people who are 20, we have people who are 80," he says.

While both agents agree that Los Angeles typically isn't a "condo market,"—with wealthy people historically preferring grand estates on large plots of land—it is becoming one.

Wildfires, the difficulty and expense of procuring insurance, and the expense and challenges of managing staff and maintenance, means that full service condos are becoming much more in demand.

"You have to show buyers that they aren't giving up amenities," says Ensani. "They are used to sceening and entertainment rooms. You have to show them they are gaining services, and someone else will take care of them for you.".

According to recent reports, penthouse E, which is even larger than Penthouse C, spanning 5,817 interior square feet and 2,442 square feet of private outdoor space, will soon hit the market. The price hasn't been released.

The American Hospital Association (AHA) and West Health Institute announced Tuesday a new collaboration with medtech tech giant Becton, Dickinson and Company (BD) aimed at accelerating the adoption of technologies shown to improve patient care.

The collaboration builds on the West Health Accelerator at AHA’s Health Research & Educational Trust (HRET), a three-year initiative to aid healthcare organizations in scaling technology-enabled solutions.

According to recent reports, “No single organization can close the gap between innovation and everyday care on its own,” noted Zia Agha, M.D., West Health Institute chief medical officer, in a statement. “This collaboration brings hospital reach, clinical technology expertise and performance intelligence together from the start. We’re beginning with a focused group of hospitals, learning what it takes to make changes last, and building a model that can reach hospitals of every size and resource level.”.

The new collaboration will begin with an initial cohort of 10 hospitals and health systems. It will incorporate advanced physiologic monitoring with clinical protocols in practice, specifically targeting complications associated with postoperative complications and longer hospital stays. Additionally, Vizient will provide performance benchmarking and analytic capabilities, the organizations stated.

Takeaways from the early cohort will help to identify adoption barriers, refine implementation approaches and outline necessary support to expand the model to a broader group.

BD Advanced Patient Monitoring Worldwide President Tim Patz said in a statement that the company believes innovation “has the greatest impact when it translates into meaningful improvements in patient care.”.

It has been revealed that “Our experience working with healthcare systems has shown us the value of bringing together advanced hemodynamic monitoring, data and the expertise of hospital care teams to support better-informed patient care,” Patz noted. “This collaboration gives us an opportunity to build on that experience, further integrate proven solutions into clinical practice and help more patients benefit from them.”.

Payer mix, non-labor expenses dragged hospital margins in September" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Hospitals’ operations took another dip in September amid a slew of ongoing headwinds including weakened payer mix and rising costs, healthcare advisory firm Kaufman Hall reported alongside warnings of a “historically large portion” of the nation’s hospitals running on negative or near-zero operating margins.

The firm’s latest monthly benchmark report, released Tuesday, highlighted a calendar year-to-date operating margin index of 1.4% and a single-month operating margin index of 2.4% in September, the latter of which was a decline from August’s 3.0% operating margin (all including health system allocations for shared services costs).

According to recent reports, the performance decline wasn’t for want of patients. Daily discharges and adjusted discharges both rose 3% from August to September, and are generally above the numbers from last year. Operating room minutes per calendar day also rose 6% from August—an encouraging sign for hospitals whose surgical slowdowns had hamstrung acuity—but remain 1% below September of last year.

According to recent reports, the increased foot traffic also grew revenues, with daily net operating revenue rising 4% from August and 6% year over year while gross operating revenue rose 4% month to month and 8% year over year. Much of the increase came on the outpatient side, where daily revenue increased 5% from August and 10% compared to September 2025. Net patient service revenue per adjusted discharge was more mixed, rising 2% from August but remaining 1% below September 2025.

However, hospitals’ margins are being challenged by persistent bad debt and charity care burdens, Kaufman Hall’s data show. Daily bad debt and charity care may have remained flat from August, but is 17% higher than September 2025 and 16% higher when comparing both years’ first nine months. As a percentage of gross operating revenue, they’re 6% higher than Sept. 2025 and 8% higher year to date.

On the spending side, daily total expense rose 3% from August and is 5% higher than September 2025, primarily reflecting the heightened volumes even as hospitals held their average length of stay flat month over month or 1% shorter year over year. The expenses were more pronounced on the non-labor side, where increases on a per adjusted discharge basis were higher than labor’s per adjusted discharge decline.

It has been revealed that "Hospitals continue to operate in an environment marked by significant financial variability," Erik Swanson, managing director and Data and Analytics group leader at Kaufman Hall, said in a release. “Many organizations continue to face mounting pressure from uncompensated care and rising expenses, underscoring the importance of proactive operational and financial strategies that build long-term resilience.".

Another amplifying market trend is the “bifurcation of hospital performance” often highlighted by the firm and others that monitor multi-organization financial trends, such as credit rating agencies.

In a recent development, "The margin gap between higher and lower-performing hospitals has widened to 19 percentage points, with a historically large portion of hospitals operating at negative or very thin margins,” the report reads. “Even slight revenue reductions threaten organizations, which face increasingly difficult decisions on future operations, care delivery, and expense control.”.

The firm encouraged hospitals to take “deliberate, proactive steps” to strengthen their financial situations, particularly as macro reimbursement trends stiffen and the site of care delivery shifts from the hospital to outpatient settings.

Kaufman Hall’s hospital reports pull data from more than 1,300 nationwide hospitals as collected by parent organization Strata Decision Technology.

Accompanying the monthly hospital benchmark was also Kaufman Hall’s quarterly numbers on more than 200,000 employed physicians and advanced practice providers, which painted a much rosier picture for health system and hospital employers.

It showed, for the first time in five years of data collection, that healthcare employers’ investment/subsidy per provider and per physician has declined year over year (by 1%), and “across every cohort, including primary care, medical specialty, surgical specialty and hospital-based specialty.”.

Kaufman Hall attributed the rare turnaround to revenue growth and sustained productivity increases that together outpaced expenses.

Sources indicate that "Medical groups made meaningful performance improvements this quarter, achieving gains in revenue, productivity and thoughtful workforce management," Matthew Bates, managing director and Physician Enterprise Service Line leader at Kaufman Hall, stated in a release. "The growing utilization of [advanced practice providers] and ongoing focus on operational and team effectiveness are helping organizations manage financial pressures while increasing access to care.”.

Tech Report: Common supplement could help fight psoriasis, scientists discover

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (917 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that A widely available nutritional supplement derived from vitamin B5 may offer a promising upcoming approach to treating psoriasis, according to research from China.
  • The findings, published October 27 in the Journal of Experimental Medicine (JEM), reveal an unexpected connection between cholesterol production and the immune system.
  • How Overactive Immune Cells Contribute to Psoriasis.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A widely available nutritional supplement derived from vitamin B5 may offer a promising upcoming approach to treating psoriasis, according to research from China. Scientists found that pantethine can calm immune cells involved in autoimmune inflammation, preventing psoriasis from developing in mice and improving symptoms in a small human clinical trial.

The findings, published October 27 in the Journal of Experimental Medicine (JEM), reveal an unexpected connection between cholesterol production and the immune system. By interfering with this process, pantethine may help reduce the excessive immune activity responsible for psoriasis and potentially other autoimmune diseases.

How Overactive Immune Cells Contribute to Psoriasis.

At the center of the discovery are dendritic cells, specialized immune cells that help organize the body's defenses. These cells act as coordinators, identifying potential threats and directing other immune cells to respond.

Sources indicate that dendritic cells perform this role by capturing foreign substances called antigens and presenting them to T cells, which are immune cells that recognize specific threats. They also release chemical signals that recruit additional immune cells and trigger inflammation.

Although these activities are essential for fighting infections, problems can arise when dendritic cells become excessively active. Instead of helping protect the body, they can contribute to persistent inflammation and autoimmune diseases such as psoriasis.

"Emerging evidence highlights that metabolic pathways and their associated metabolites play vital roles in regulating immune cell function and autoimmune progression," says Wei-Na Zhang, a researcher at the State Key Laboratory of Biomedical Analysis in Beijing. "But therapeutic strategies targeting metabolism in inflammatory diseases remain underexplored.".

Zhang led the research alongside Qing Xia, Ai-Ling Li, and Tao Zhou, also from the State Key Laboratory of Biomedical Analysis, and Cheng-Xin Li from The First Medical Center of Chinese PLA General Hospital in Beijing.

Scientists Discover a Hidden Link Between Cholesterol and Psoriasis.

The researchers identified unusually high levels of enzymes called Vanins in dendritic cells from people with psoriasis and several other autoimmune diseases. These enzymes help regulate the processing of certain substances involved in cellular metabolism.

When the scientists reduced Vanin levels, dendritic cells became less active and were less capable of stimulating T cells. They also found that a drug designed to inhibit Vanins prevented psoriasis from developing in mice.

Further investigation revealed why these enzymes might play such an notable role.

Vanins convert pantethine into vitamin B5, an essential nutrient that cells need to produce energy. Pantethine is already sold as a nutritional supplement and is commonly used to help lower blood cholesterol because it can reduce cholesterol production.

It has been revealed that this connection is particularly interesting because cholesterol does more than circulate in the bloodstream. It also influences how immune cells function. Previous research has shown that cholesterol can stimulate dendritic cell activity, while elevated blood cholesterol is a major risk factor for developing psoriasis.

Recent findings suggest that the team discovered that excessive Vanin activity reduces the amount of pantethine available inside dendritic cells. As pantethine levels fall, cholesterol production increases, causing these immune cells to become unusually active.

Sources indicate that restoring pantethine levels interrupted this process. The supplement reduced cholesterol accumulation within dendritic cells and helped suppress the excessive immune activation associated with inflammation.

"We found that pantethine administration effectively alleviated psoriasis in mice, suggesting that insufficient pantethine levels may be the crucial contributor to hyperactivation of dendritic cells and autoimmune inflammation following the up-regulation of Vanins," Zhang states.

Common Supplement Demonstrates Promise in Human Psoriasis Trial.

Encouraged by the laboratory and animal findings, the researchers investigated whether pantethine might also benefit people living with psoriasis.

They conducted a small clinical trial involving 24 patients with the condition. All participants received a topical ointment containing calcipotriene/betamethasone, a combination treatment used to control psoriasis symptoms. Calcipotriene is a vitamin D derivative that helps regulate skin cell growth, while betamethasone is a corticosteroid that reduces inflammation.

Half of the participants also took pantethine tablets, allowing researchers to examine whether adding the supplement improved the results of standard treatment.

Industry observers note that after 12 weeks, the patients who received pantethine alongside their prescribed ointment showed greater improvement in psoriasis symptoms. The benefits were especially noticeable among participants who had high blood cholesterol levels before treatment.

These findings suggest that pantethine could potentially serve as an additional treatment for psoriasis, particularly in patients whose cholesterol metabolism may be contributing to inflammation.

However, the trial included only 24 people, and the researchers emphasize that larger studies are necessary to confirm the supplement's effectiveness. The human results also do not establish that the same biological mechanism observed in laboratory experiments is responsible for the improvement in patients.

"Our investigator-initiated clinical trial demonstrated encouraging therapeutic efficacy of pantethine as an adjunctive therapy in psoriasis, but these findings should be interpreted as proof-of-concept for clinical feasibility rather than direct mechanistic validation," Zhang says. "Overall, our study uncovers the Vanin-pantethine-cholestrol axis as a key metabolic pathway governing dendritic cell activation and provides a foundation for therapeutic strategies targeting several dendritic cell-mediated autoimmune diseases.".

Less than half (42.2%) of patients say communications from healthcare providers “often” or “always” feel relevant to their needs, a new report from Lirio found.

Analysts at the behavioral science and AI-powered behavioral intelligence platform polled 1,500 adults across the U.S. for the survey. While 58% of respondents report communications not consistently feeling relevant to their needs, 55.6% rate overall communication experiences with healthcare organizations as “good” or “excellent.”.

When asked why healthcare communications are ignored altogether, respondents report generic or irrelevant content (24.4%), too many similar messages (21.8%) and confusing, jargon-filled messages (18.8%) as top reasons.

Nearly half of respondents (47.9%) report the potential value of more personalized, better-timed messages as an “8, 9 or 10” for how much it could help them make better care decisions and stay engaged.

Lirio Chief Behavioral Officer Amy Bucher, Ph.D., stated in a statement patients “are not rejecting healthcare communications outright.”.

“They are telling us, in specific and measurable terms, that the system is talking at them instead of to them,” Bucher noted. "The instinct in healthcare has long been to solve engagement with more outreach - more emails, more reminders, more portals. This data demonstrates that volume is not the problem. What is missing is relevance — content and timing designed for where a specific patient is in their own health journey, rather than a single message broadcast to an entire population.”.

Bucher added the healthcare organizations that close the communication gap will be “the ones that use behavioral data to determine the right message, the right channel, and the right moment for each individual patient, which is the model Lirio was built to deliver.".

#53595. Industry News: Scientists finally discover why we learn to love bitter coffee

Industry News: Scientists finally discover why we learn to love bitter coffee

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1327 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that A first taste of black coffee can be surprisingly unpleasant.
  • It has been revealed that scientists at UC San Francisco may have uncovered an important part of the answer.
  • Sources indicate that dopamine is a chemical messenger involved in motivation, reward, and learning.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A first taste of black coffee can be surprisingly unpleasant. Its sharp bitterness is the kind of flavor our brains are naturally inclined to avoid. Yet millions of people eventually come to enjoy that same taste, often looking forward to their morning cup. What changes?

It has been revealed that scientists at UC San Francisco may have uncovered an important part of the answer. Their research reveals a little-understood dopamine pathway linking the digestive system and the brain, helping explain how we develop a liking for certain flavors through repeated experience.

Sources indicate that dopamine is a chemical messenger involved in motivation, reward, and learning. Researchers have long known that it helps the brain recognize experiences worth repeating. However, most studies have examined rapid dopamine signals that appear within seconds of encountering something rewarding, such as the sight of a favorite meal.

The latest research, published November 4 in Nature, examines a different system. This slower pathway responds to information coming from inside the body, allowing the brain to learn about the benefits of food after it has been consumed.

"We've shown that this slow dopamine system is what drives us to learn to like certain foods over time, and we can see where and how that happens," mentioned Zachary Knight, PhD, professor of Physiology and senior author of the study.

The findings offer a possible explanation for why an initially unpleasant flavor can gradually become enjoyable. Once the brain connects the taste of coffee with caffeine's stimulating effects, Knight explained, "that coffee starts to taste a lot better.".

How the Gut Sends Reward Signals to the Brain.

Scientists have spent decades investigating dopamine and its influence on behavior. Its familiar, rapidly acting signals help us respond to opportunities for reward. But dopamine also operates on a slower timescale, through a system that has received far less attention.

According to Knight, this slower process largely unfolds outside our conscious awareness.

In a recent development, when food enters the digestive tract, specialized sensors detect nutrients, including sugar and fat. Information about those nutrients travels toward the brain, where it can produce a dopamine response that develops gradually and continues for several minutes.

Recent findings suggest that to investigate this process, Knight worked with James Grove, PhD, who was a graduate student at the time. They introduced nutrients directly into the stomachs of mice while monitoring dopamine activity throughout their brains.

The researchers used either sugar water or a liquid resembling a milkshake. Delivering these substances directly into the stomach allowed them to separate the effects of nutrients from the experience of tasting food.

The results revealed a powerful, prolonged dopamine response in a specific brain region called the anterior basolateral amygdala, or BLA.

In a recent development, the amygdala is involved in emotional processing and learning, including forming associations between experiences and their consequences. Scientists already knew that dopamine was released in this particular region, but its purpose had remained unclear.

"We could see that this dopamine is part of a different system and begin to understand its role," he said.

Scientists Find a Brain Circuit That Changes Food Preferences.

Finding the dopamine signal was only the beginning. The researchers next wanted to determine whether it actually influenced how animals learned to prefer different flavors.

They first interrupted the newly identified pathway in mice. The animals continued eating normally, indicating that the disruption did not prevent them from consuming food. However, they lost the ability to learn that an unfamiliar flavor was associated with receiving calories.

The team then conducted the opposite experiment.

After mice tasted a flavor containing no calories, the researchers artificially activated dopamine fibers in the BLA. Remarkably, the animals developed a preference for that flavor even though it provided no nutritional reward.

In effect, stimulating the pathway reproduced the learning signal that nutrients would ordinarily generate.

Together, the experiments showed that this dopamine system plays a critical role in teaching the brain which flavors predict rewarding nutritional effects.

A Surprising Discovery in the Left Side of the Brain.

Industry observers note that the researchers also looked for evidence that a comparable process occurs in humans. Brain imaging studies conducted by Knight's collaborators revealed a strikingly similar pattern.

Recent findings suggest that dana Small, PhD, a psychologist at Yale University, revisited data from an earlier positron emission tomography (PET) study involving 13 men. Participants had consumed either a milkshake or a drink without calories.

Her analysis found that dopamine release following nutrient delivery was especially concentrated in the left side of the BLA.

It has been revealed that A separate study led by Marc Tittgemeyer, PhD, and his colleagues provided additional evidence. Using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), which measures changes in brain activity associated with blood flow, the researchers examined 38 adults after they consumed glucose, a simple sugar.

They observed increased activity in the same brain region.

One of the most unexpected findings was that the response was not evenly distributed between the brain's two hemispheres.

In both mice and humans, nutrients produced a considerably stronger dopamine response in the left BLA than in the corresponding region on the right.

That imbalance surprised Knight because brain networks responsible for essential functions, such as feeding, are generally expected to work in a relatively symmetrical fashion.

Industry observers note that why the left side plays such a prominent role remains unanswered. Knight's laboratory is now investigating what causes this unusual difference.

Could This Discovery Help Scientists Change Food Cravings?

Sources indicate that identifying the pathway provides researchers with a clearer picture of how the digestive system influences the brain's learned responses to food. It also raises an intriguing possibility: Could scientists eventually use this knowledge to change which foods people find appealing?

One area of interest involves GLP-1 medications, a class of drugs that mimic a hormone naturally released by the gut. These medications can substantially alter appetite and eating behavior.

Knight's team did not investigate GLP-1 drugs in the new study, so it remains unknown whether they influence the dopamine pathway the researchers identified.

Still, Knight suggests that one possible explanation for some of their effects could involve reducing the dopamine signals generated when nutrients reach the digestive system. If that happens, foods might gradually become less rewarding because the brain would receive weaker signals reinforcing their flavors.

For now, this remains a hypothesis rather than a demonstrated effect of the medications.

The broader implications extend beyond hunger and fullness. Many approaches to changing eating behavior focus on reducing appetite or increasing feelings of satisfaction after a meal. The newly mapped pathway suggests that the brain's process of learning food preferences could eventually become another target.

By influencing how the brain connects flavors with their consequences, future treatments might someday help people develop different preferences rather than simply making them feel less hungry.

"By understanding the steps between nutrient detection in the gut and learning in the brain, it might be possible to fine-tune them to subtly change our preferences for different foods," Knight noted.

Recent findings suggest that the discovery offers a latest perspective on why our tastes can change over time. From learning to enjoy bitter coffee to developing a preference for calorie-rich foods, what we love to eat may depend partly on a quiet conversation between the gut and brain that continues long after the first bite.

The research was supported by the National Institutes of Health (grants R01-DK106399, R01-DK138127, R01-NS116626, and R01-DK145100 and F31-NS120468).

Teladoc Health is expanding its Comprehensive Weight Care program with a new option that allows employers to contribute to GLP-1 costs outside of traditional pharmacy benefit designs.

Through the new offering, employers can give access to medications from Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk—accompanied by support from licensed professionals, personalized lifestyle coaching, artificial intelligence-enabled food logging and more.

Sources indicate that with each plan year, employers will set a fixed payment per employee per fill that applies consistently across covered medications, the tech giant said. Employees then pay the remaining balance for each fill. Teladoc manages eligibility, program oversight and consolidated invoicing.

Pharmacy claims are administered on a 100% pass-through basis, including eligibility verification and audit-ready claims documentation.

Moreover, employers can opt in to tie contributions to program engagement, using metrics like food logging and regular weigh-ins, executives say.

Recent findings suggest that the offering is available now, with initial contracted clients slated to launch programs for their employees beginning Jan. 1, 2027.

Industry observers note that “Employers want to provide benefits that help their workforce achieve their health goals and need flexible strategies that work for their organizations,” said Kelly Bliss, Teladoc Health U.S. Group Health president, in a statement. “We are helping employers meet the needs of their employees while providing greater predictability and transparency around healthcare spending. Importantly, we give people a trusted path to high-quality care and affordable access to FDA-approved, authentic medication for meaningful, sustained health outcomes.”.

Alongside the announcement, the organization also unveiled new research examining two years of weight-loss outcomes among nearly 23,000 members enrolled in its programs.

Results indicated “clinically meaningful weight loss” increased over time, with 47.7% of members achieving at least 5% weight loss by 24 months. And among those who lost weight during their first year, 53% continued losing additional weight during the second.

Singer Ella Langley made history at the Country Music Awards when she set the record for the most CMA awards won by a woman in one night—so will where the hitmaker house her latest trophies?

The "Choosin Texas" singer, 27, won entertainer of the year, female vocalist of the year, album of the year, single of the year, and song of the year.

When accepting her sixth award of the evening, she teased, "At this point, I'm sick of me!".

“This has been the most special night. I could quit tomorrow and have the best career of my life," she added.

At one point during the evening, fellow country star Lainey Wilson joked, "I noted I was gonna bring you a bedazzled broom. I knew you was gonna sweep, girl.”.

At the end of the evening, Langley posed with all of her awards as she smiled from ear to ear.

Langley will put her multiple trophies on display at her lakefront retreat, which she picked up in 2025.

In July 2025, Langley snapped up her first-ever home in her hometown of Montgomery, AL, just minutes away from her parents' home.

Langley, who lives in Nashville, TN, but was born and raised in Alabama, gushed about her newly minted purchase while speaking to Audacy, telling the radio station that she decided to make her first real estate investment in her home state because she feels most like herself when she's there.

It has been revealed that "It just brings me back to who I am at the root of me every time I go back there. And when it comes to writing songs and being in that state of mind, I think it’s important to have a place like that," she stated.

The star noted that, while she will likely "always" live in Tennessee, which is the home of country music, she will continue to keep roots in Alabama because of how close she is to her family.

“I think I’ll always have to live in Tennessee to some extent in my life, but being from Alabama, it’s so close. It’s under four hours to get there," she added.

Though many young people might find the process of buying their first property overwhelming, Langley conceded that she was in a much more privileged position—namely because she has her own business managers who helped to oversee the entire purchase.

"I honestly been having a blast. I have great business management. They just get all the phone calls, yes or no, this is what I want to do, and they figure out all the little logistics, so very thankful for them,” she added.

Langley moved to Nashville in order to pursue her musical career, relocating from her hometown in Alabama in 2019.

"The music family here is just really special; people are so willing to be a mentor or help you grow in a way I just couldn’t do back home," Langley mentioned of her fresh home state during an interview with Raised Rowdy.

Previously, Langley has shared that her move to Nashville also helped her to find more freedom in her writing process, joking to Raised Rowdy that she spent much of her childhood in Alabama trying to "survive life" with two brothers.

"I grew up in the country in Alabama between two brothers, so a lot of my childhood was just trying to survive life between those two," she said.

"I always was trying to prove I was just as tough and fearless as they were. Being a tomboy like that, a lot of my friends ended up being guys. If you ask my band or people who know me, they’ll tell you sometimes I seem more like a guy than a girl. But I think women can still be direct, strong, and tough, without apologizing for who they are or how they think.".

Making the decision to pursue her music full time was a serious one for Langley, who dropped out of Auburn University in order to focus on her passion.

“I had a boyfriend who was in music and then his manager, they were both moving to Nashville and we’re going to live with Trey (Lewis). And I was like, well hell, I’m not staying here," she previously told CountryNow.

In a recent development, "So I called mom and dad and I remarked, ‘Hey, I think I want to drop out of school and move to Nashville. I’m just going to be in more debt anyways when I graduate. I mean, I’m going to go do this anyways. I would rather start it now.'".

The singer also revealed that she was warmly welcomed to Nashville.

According to recent reports, “It’s been a cool journey of finding those people for me in town that I just love and love me and believe in me and I believe in them. And so that’s what’s really kept me going a lot through this," she went on.

"And obviously my family supports me the way that they do and just love me, but that’s the thing, nobody has ever thought I was going to do anything else ….

"If you ask any of my family, they’re like, ‘Yeah, we all knew that this was what she was going to do.’ So there wasn’t ever really any question when I wanted to move.".

#53591. Tech Report: Alzheimer’s may have early warning signs outside the brain

Tech Report: Alzheimer’s may have early warning signs outside the brain

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1464 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Alzheimer's disease is best known for its effects on memory and thinking, but newly introduced research suggests that some symptoms may develop in a surprising place: outside the brain.
  • Scientists at the University of Central Florida (UCF) have discovered that genetic mutations associated with Alzheimer's can interfere with the nerves that control muscle movement, even without involvement from the brain or spinal cord.
  • The discovery raises the possibility that movement difficulties could provide earlier warning signs of the disease and that treatments focused exclusively on the brain may overlook important problems elsewhere in the body.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Alzheimer's disease is best known for its effects on memory and thinking, but newly introduced research suggests that some symptoms may develop in a surprising place: outside the brain.

Scientists at the University of Central Florida (UCF) have discovered that genetic mutations associated with Alzheimer's can interfere with the nerves that control muscle movement, even without involvement from the brain or spinal cord. The findings could help explain why some people with Alzheimer's experience changes in walking, balance, or coordination long before noticeable memory problems emerge.

The discovery raises the possibility that movement difficulties could provide earlier warning signs of the disease and that treatments focused exclusively on the brain may overlook important problems elsewhere in the body.

Industry observers note that the research was led by James Hickman, a professor at UCF's Nanoscience Technology Center, and Research Professor Xiufang "Nadine" Guo, working alongside scientists at the healthcare technology company Hesperos. Funded by the National Institutes of Health's National Institute on Aging, the study used laboratory systems built from human cells to investigate how inherited Alzheimer's mutations affect movement. The findings were published in Alzheimer's & Dementia: The Journal of the Alzheimer's Association.

Industry observers note that "Motor deficits may be an earlier indication [of Alzheimer's]," Guo says. "If we can detect those changes and intervene earlier, that could help delay the onset of central nervous system symptoms.".

Why Alzheimer's Symptoms May Appear Before Memory Loss.

Alzheimer's is generally associated with progressive memory loss, confusion, and declining cognitive abilities. However, doctors have also observed that some patients develop physical symptoms, including changes in balance, coordination, and gait (manner of walking), years before clear cognitive difficulties become apparent.

These observations have raised an important question: Are such movement problems simply a consequence of damage occurring in the brain, or could Alzheimer's also interfere directly with nerves elsewhere in the body?

To investigate, the UCF team focused on familial Alzheimer's, a rare inherited form of the disease that typically develops earlier in life (from 40 to 65 years of age) than the more common form.

Their experiments revealed that motor neurons carrying mutations linked to familial Alzheimer's could disrupt the connections responsible for controlling muscles, even when the brain and spinal cord were completely absent from the experimental system.

It has been revealed that motor neurons are specialized nerve cells that transmit signals to muscles, telling them when to contract and produce movement. The new findings suggest that Alzheimer's mutations can interfere with this process directly, rather than affecting movement only through damage to the brain.

"This is the first time it's been demonstrated that deficits in the peripheral nervous system can arise directly from these mutations," Hickman indicates. "It means drugs that target the brain may not fix problems in the rest of the body.".

It has been revealed that the peripheral nervous system includes the nerves located outside the brain and spinal cord. These nerves carry signals between the central nervous system and the rest of the body, helping control movement, sensation, and other essential functions.

Recent findings suggest that guo also points out that preserving the ability to move could have benefits beyond physical health. Regular physical activity is associated with better cognitive well-being, so protecting motor function may also help support brain health.

How a Miniature Human Cell System Revealed the Discovery.

To examine the relationship between Alzheimer's mutations and muscle movement, the scientists used an innovative laboratory platform known as "human-on-a-chip" technology.

Developed and manufactured through Hesperos, a tech giant co-founded by Hickman, these miniature systems bring different types of human cells together under controlled conditions. They allow researchers to recreate specific biological functions and observe how diseases interfere with them.

Recent findings suggest that unlike conventional laboratory experiments that examine isolated cells, these systems can reproduce crucial interactions between different tissues. They also provide an alternative to animal models, which do not always accurately reflect how human diseases behave.

For this study, the team created a miniature model of the neuromuscular junction, the connection where a motor neuron communicates with a muscle cell.

The model was deliberately designed without a brain or spinal cord. This was a crucial part of the experiment because it allowed the researchers to investigate whether Alzheimer's-related changes could cause movement problems independently of the central nervous system.

It has been revealed that the scientists combined healthy muscle cells with motor neurons derived from stem cells that carried genetic mutations associated with familial Alzheimer's disease. Stem cells are cells that can develop into specialized types of cells, making them valuable tools for studying human diseases in the laboratory.

The researchers then examined how effectively the altered nerve cells communicated with otherwise healthy muscle tissue.

The results indicated that the Alzheimer's-associated mutations could interfere with normal nerve-to-muscle function. This suggests that at least some movement difficulties linked to the disease may arise directly in the peripheral nervous system rather than being caused entirely by degeneration in the brain.

Why Damaged Nerve Connections Can Affect Walking and Balance.

Every voluntary movement depends on successful communication between the nervous system and the muscles.

Sources indicate that at the neuromuscular junction, an electrical signal traveling along a motor neuron triggers chemical communication that causes a muscle to contract. This process makes everyday activities possible, from walking and maintaining posture to lifting objects and performing precise movements.

When the connection becomes impaired, muscles may respond less effectively to nerve signals. Depending on the severity and location of the problem, this can contribute to weakness, reduced coordination, and difficulty sustaining physical activity.

To evaluate these effects, the research team measured how consistently nerve signals produced muscle contractions and how long the muscles could continue contracting before becoming fatigued.

These measurements provided a direct assessment of how well the nerve and muscle cells worked together. They also resemble aspects of the functional testing physicians use when examining patients with movement disorders.

Recent findings suggest that "You can't move unless the motor circuit works," Hickman claims. "When a doctor taps your knee to check your reflex, they're testing that exact connection.".

By demonstrating impaired nerve-to-muscle communication in a system containing no brain or spinal cord, the study provides evidence that mutations linked to familial Alzheimer's can produce effects beyond the central nervous system.

Sources indicate that however, the experiments do not establish that these changes necessarily occur before memory loss in patients. Further research will be needed to determine how closely the laboratory findings reflect the progression of Alzheimer's in people, particularly those with the more common forms of the disease.

Could This Discovery Lead to Earlier Alzheimer's Detection?

The findings suggest a potentially important new direction for Alzheimer's research: looking beyond memory and other cognitive symptoms when investigating the disease.

If future studies confirm that changes in motor function are detectable early in certain patients, tests of walking, coordination, or nerve-to-muscle activity might eventually help identify disease-related changes before more obvious neurological symptoms develop.

The results also raise questions about treatment. Many Alzheimer's therapies are designed to address processes occurring in the brain, but medications that target the central nervous system may not necessarily correct abnormalities affecting peripheral nerves and muscles.

Understanding these separate effects could help researchers investigate treatments that protect physical function alongside cognitive health.

Human-on-a-Chip Technology Could Transform Disease Research.

Beyond the implications for Alzheimer's, the researchers see considerable potential in using human-on-a-chip systems to investigate other diseases and evaluate possible treatments.

Because these platforms contain human cells and reproduce measurable biological activities, they can help scientists observe disease-related changes in conditions that more closely resemble human physiology than some conventional experimental models.

This approach may be particularly useful in drug development, where researchers need to understand not only how a potential treatment affects individual cells but also how it influences interactions between different tissues.

Such systems can also uncover biological effects that may be difficult to detect in animal experiments, potentially helping researchers identify promising therapies and recognize limitations earlier in development.

For Hickman, the progress represents the culmination of three decades of work devoted to understanding disease through more realistic laboratory models.

"These systems let us study disease in a way that's closer to what actually happens in the human body, and that's what we need to develop better treatments," he says.

Materials provided by University of Central Florida. Original written by Emily Dougherty. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

Earlier this year, Optum Rx teased the rollout of new pharmacy tools designed to address medication cost and access.

Now, the company is offering a look at how those tools work.

The pharmacy benefit manager stated Tuesday that the tools build on Optum's latest and more transparent pharmacy model, which the company confirmed in May and shifts to a fee-based structure. The model moves away from more traditional approaches linked to manufacturer pricing and prescription volume and offers clients a clearly defined fee structure.

In a recent development, the first platform, called Shop MyScript, allows members to compare prices for their medications as well as their options for pharmacies or delivery before the prescription is dispensed. The tool will notify members of potential cost savings shortly after a script is written.

In addition, Shop MyScript embeds in the prescribing workflow, Optum mentioned, so that the member does not have to make comparisons after the fact. If they choose to keep the existing prescription, it will then be sent to the pharmacy.

Optum noted that early adopters have averaged $28 in savings through the program.

Sources indicate that "People should have clear information about their medication costs and options when they can actually use it, not after a decision has already been made," said Katte Carey, president of Optum Rx, in the announcement. "These tools give people more information earlier in their journey, so they can make choices that work for them and get the support they need along the way.".

In addition, the pharmacy benefit manager confirmed Optum Assistant, a conversational AI guide that helps members complete routine tasks and track down key information. The tool can triage concerns on a range of topics, from questions about medication and benefits to pharmacy experience challenges.

If the AI guide can't address the individual's needs, they can choose to be connected to live support to find a solution. Optum said about 80% of conversations using the tool led to a resolution without needing a live advocate.

The final fresh launch aims to support cash-pay options, according to the announcement.

According to recent reports, optum Price Wise will offer members a complete cost breakdown, including the price of a drug and any fees. That total, all-in price allows members to fully understand what their options may be and make the choice that works best for them at the pharmacy counter.

Recent findings suggest that the PBM noted newly introduced tools like these build on Optum's new and more transparent pharmacy model, which the company confirmed in May and shifts to a fee-based structure. The model moves away from more traditional approaches linked to manufacturer pricing and prescription volume and offers clients a clearly defined fee structure.

Medicare Shared Savings Program saved $2.5B last year: CMS" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The Medicare Shared Savings Program has reached the highest savings number in its history, according to new federal data.

The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services noted Tuesday that the program generated more than $2.5 billion in net savings for Medicare in 2025, making for the ninth year in a row that it led to cost savings. The agency added that every accountable care organization met or exceeded quality reporting requirements.

ACOs participating in MSSP earned $4.9 billion in shared savings payments during 2025, CMS mentioned, with 80% of organizations earning performance payments.

As of 2026, 511 ACOs representing more than 700,000 providers are participating in the Medicare Shared Savings Program, which represents 12.6 million people enrolled in traditional Medicare, another record.

It has been revealed that "Patients want doctors who work together, care that puts their needs first, and fewer unnecessary hurdles—that is what accountable care is designed to deliver," mentioned CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz, M.D., in the announcement. "These record savings show the power of rewarding providers for quality and coordination. We want more people with Medicare, and more of the providers who care for them, to benefit from this approach.".

CMS said that it wants to make it easier for providers to participate in MSSP if they choose, especially given the program's results to date. It included changes in the latest Physician Fee Schedule to encourage participation, including increased opportunity for certain ACOs to earn shared savings and fresh financial incentives to draw in first-time participants.

It has been revealed that in addition, CMS remarked that would create more predictable spending targets that make planning and participation straightforward. The agency is also aiming to streamline patient notices and simplify required technology.

“We are excited to see continued progress on both savings and enrollment for Medicare beneficiaries. Beneficiaries are best served when a provider is watching out for them and coordinating their care,” noted Center for Medicare Director John Brooks in the announcement.

Emily Brower, CEO of the National Association of ACOs, said in a statement that the 2025 results "build on years of progress and underscore what the accountable care community can accomplish through collaboration, innovation and the widespread adoption of proven best practices.".

It has been revealed that "NAACOS looks forward to partnering with CMS to build on this momentum," stated Brower. "Policies that unleash innovation, reduce burden, and create sustainability through fair and predictable budgets will allow ACOs to deliver even greater value for patients and the Medicare program.".

#53587. Obesity linked to up to 27% lower risk of death in dementia

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1298 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Obesity linked to up to 27% lower risk of death in dementia

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1298 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A surprising new study has found that people who are overweight or obese when diagnosed with dementia tend to live longer than those who have a normal body weight.
  • Researchers from Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health and NYU School of Global Public Health found that body weight at the time of diagnosis may provide important clues about how long someone with dementia is likely to live.
  • Sources indicate that the results are particularly intriguing because obesity is well established as a risk factor for several serious health problems, including heart disease and diabetes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A surprising new study has found that people who are overweight or obese when diagnosed with dementia tend to live longer than those who have a normal body weight. The findings challenge expectations about the relationship between weight and health, suggesting that carrying extra weight may be associated with an unexpected survival advantage after dementia develops.

Researchers from Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health and NYU School of Global Public Health found that body weight at the time of diagnosis may provide important clues about how long someone with dementia is likely to live. Their findings, published in the Journal of Alzheimer's Disease, also highlight the importance of proper nutrition for people living with the condition.

Sources indicate that the results are particularly intriguing because obesity is well established as a risk factor for several serious health problems, including heart disease and diabetes. Being overweight or obese during middle age is also associated with a greater likelihood of developing dementia later in life. However, previous research has suggested that the relationship may reverse once dementia has developed, with higher body weight linked to better survival.

"Because this finding is somewhat counterintuitive, an important question is whether it could simply be an artifact of bias. Our analyses suggest that the major sources of bias we examined do not explain the survival advantage associated with higher weight," remarked corresponding author Yuan Zhang, PhD, assistant professor of Sociomedical Sciences at Columbia Mailman and in the Butler Columbia Aging Center.

Obesity Linked to Up to 27% Lower Risk of Death.

Sources indicate that the researchers found substantial differences in survival based on body weight at the time of dementia diagnosis. Compared with individuals in the normal weight range, those who were overweight or obese had a significantly lower risk of death, even after the researchers accounted for smoking, existing medical conditions, and demographic characteristics.

In a recent development, people classified as overweight (body mass index of 25 to 29.9) had a 16 percent lower risk of death. Those with class 1 obesity (BMI of 30 to 34.9) had an even larger reduction of 27 percent, while individuals with class 2 and 3 obesity (BMI equal to or greater than 35) had a 22 percent lower risk.

Despite these striking differences, the researchers caution that the findings should not be interpreted as a recommendation for people with dementia to gain weight.

"This doesn't mean that patients with dementia should attempt to become overweight or obese, as our study was not designed to test that question. But our findings do suggest that weight status may serve as a useful prognostic signal for survival at the time of dementia diagnosis. They also support the notion that nutrition is a key factor in the health and survival of people with dementia," mentioned Virginia Chang, associate professor of Social and Behavioral Sciences at NYU School of Global Public Health and the study's first author.

Tracking Weight and Dementia Over 24 Years.

To investigate the connection, Zhang, Chang, and their colleagues examined information from the Health and Retirement Study, a nationally representative research project that follows Americans ages 51 and older.

The team analyzed records collected between 1998 and 2022, focusing on 4,523 participants who did not have dementia when they entered the study but subsequently developed the condition.

According to recent reports, because the data covered such a long period, the researchers could examine how participants' weight changed in the years leading up to their diagnosis. They could also determine their weight when dementia was identified and track their survival afterward.

According to recent reports, this extended timeline was especially vital because scientists have questioned whether the apparent benefit of higher body weight is genuine or simply reflects misleading patterns in the data. One possibility is that having additional fat or muscle gives patients resources that help them withstand the physical effects of dementia. Another is that the association arises from factors that earlier studies did not adequately consider.

Could Weight Loss Explain the Dementia Paradox?

One major concern involves weight loss that occurs before dementia becomes clinically apparent.

Earlier research by Zhang and Chang found that people can begin losing weight as much as 10 years before a dementia diagnosis, with the decline becoming more pronounced as the disease approaches.

According to recent reports, this creates a potential problem for studies that measure weight only at the time dementia is diagnosed. Some individuals classified as having a normal weight may previously have been heavier and lost weight because of the developing disease. If those individuals are already experiencing more advanced illness, they may face a greater risk of death, making higher body weight appear beneficial by comparison.

The researchers also considered other possible distortions. Restricting an analysis to people who develop dementia can create misleading relationships between obesity and mortality, even when the underlying connection is more complicated.

Recent findings suggest that another concern is known as "survivor" bias. Since people with obesity face an increased risk of dying from certain illnesses before reaching the age when dementia typically develops, those who survive long enough to receive a dementia diagnosis may represent an unusually healthy group.

To determine whether these factors explained the findings, the team performed additional analyses designed to evaluate several potential sources of bias. The results indicated that the biases they examined were unlikely to be major drivers of the observed connection between higher weight and lower mortality.

Why Extra Weight Might Help People With Dementia.

Although the precise explanation remains unknown, the researchers identified several biological reasons why additional body weight could be advantageous for someone already living with dementia.

It has been revealed that one possibility involves the body's energy reserves. People with more stored fat or greater muscle mass may be better equipped to withstand periods of poor nutrition and the physical deterioration that can accompany the disease.

Dementia can interfere with eating in several ways. Changes in brain function may reduce appetite or motivation to eat, while some patients experience increased energy needs or gradually lose the ability to feed themselves. Over time, these problems can contribute to significant weight loss, muscle wasting, and declining health.

It has been revealed that "Nutrition can be a significant problem for people with dementia," remarked Chang. "They may experience wasting and an inability to eat, which can be due to changes in the brain's central drive, leading to loss of appetite and initiative, increased energy expenditure, and difficulties feeding themselves.".

Having additional energy stores or muscle tissue could potentially help patients cope with these challenges, although the study did not establish that these factors directly explain the survival differences.

The researchers emphasize that important questions remain unanswered. Even after examining multiple potential biases and identifying plausible biological explanations, they cannot say for certain why overweight and obese participants experienced lower mortality.

Industry observers note that nevertheless, Zhang and Chang believe that weight at the time of a dementia diagnosis could provide valuable information about a patient's likely survival. The results also reinforce the importance of recognizing and addressing nutritional problems in people with dementia.

Additional study authors include Eleanor Hayes-Larson of the University of Southern California and Hui Zheng of the University of Toronto.

The research received funding from the National Institutes of Health (grant numbers R00AG070274, R00AG075317).

Heidi Overton’s FDA nomination pulled by White House" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The White House pulled the nomination for Heidi Overton, M.D., Ph.D., to lead the FDA just hours before the Senate was scheduled to vote on her confirmation.

The move hardly comes as a surprise after Overton’s confirmation hearing before the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions (HELP) Committee drew contention.

The news was first reported by Axios on Tuesday evening. The White House confirmed the news to Fierce the following morning.

In September, the HELP committee questioned Overton in a hearing marked by tightrope-walking on issues like vaccines, abortions, flavored vapes and whether or not President Donald Trump is capable of being wrong.

Overton conceded multiple times during the hearing that vaccines approved by the FDA, as well as the “abortion pill” mifepristone, are safe and effective. But she stopped short of admitting that Trump has been wrong when dispensing medical information out of line with what scientific evidence reveals.

Sources indicate that overton’s nomination faced mounting pushback and uncertainty from senators ahead of a planned HELP Committee vote on Nov. 18. Fierce reached out to Sen. Ed Markey, the veteran Democratic lawmaker from Massachusetts, ahead of the vote, and he told Fierce that he would “vote against her nomination, and I urge my colleagues to do the same.”.

“The FDA needs a leader who will stand up for science and for our kids’ safety, not one who stood by while both were undermined,” he added.

Republican Sen. Bill Cassidy of Louisiana, who chairs the Senate health committee, and other Republicans had also raised questions about Overton's nomination.

In a recent development, as support for Overton looked thin, Republicans were discussing Sen. Roger Marshall, a Kansas Republican, as a potential replacement, Semafor reported today. Health Secretary Kennedy reportedly met with Marshall in recent days to discuss filling the role, according to Politico, but the White House told the publication that it is not considering him.

Robert Steinbrook, M.D., health research group director for Public Citizen, commented today urging the HELP committee to reject Overton’s nomination: “The FDA needs a strong commissioner who stands for science and the integrity of the agency,” Steinbrook mentioned. “Overton is the wrong choice for FDA Commissioner and has done nothing to dispel the well-founded reasons to oppose her candidacy.”.

Analysts from Citi shared that the White House’s decision to pull the nomination has a negative impact on biopharma, “extending uncertainty around permanent agency leadership.”.

“We view the withdrawal as a modest sentiment negative, but not a material near-term change to the regulatory environment facing most drug and biologics sponsors,” the analysts said in the note.

Sources indicate that the withdrawal of Overton's nomination leaves a gap at an FDA that has already faced significant upheaval. The White House only shifted its focus to Overton in August, after the agency had spent three months without a permanent leader.

Since former FDA commissioner Marty Makary, M.D., departed the agency in May, Kyle Diamantas, who hails from the agency’s food regulation division, has been at the helm in an interim capacity.

According to recent reports, when it comes to exploring enticing investment opportunities, real estate often stands out as an excellent solution for making and growing wealth. There are numerous tips for getting started and ways you can start your journey into the property world, and some options are actually simpler and more affordable than you might expect. Here are some of the best, most interesting ways to invest in real estate, if you want to avoid the traditional buy and flip strategy.

According to recent reports, not all real estate investments have to include purchasing actual bricks and mortar in the physical world. The digital landscape has evolved drastically in recent years, introducing new opportunities for innovative entrepreneurs to make money buying virtual assets. According to recent reports, with digital real estate, companies purchase a section of the blockchain in a metaverse landscape, where they can build online experiences, or simply store other assets. This indicates learning how to invest in digital real estate could be a worthwhile strategy for any consumer. Even if you’re not familiar with this form of property-based investing, you probably know the term crowdfunding. The approach allows investors to participate in products that would have been impossible to access in the past because of high capital requirements. Individuals can use this strategy to diversify their portfolios with a variety of different locations and property types. Plus, you’ll earn a passive income through rental profits, and property appreciation.

Another real estate investment strategy gaining increasing attention in recent years is REITs. These are basically investment vehicles responsible for owning and operating income-generating assets, such as rental properties and office blocks. You can even use this strategy to spread your portfolio across industrial, residential, and commercial properties. They’re also a highly liquid investment option, making them appealing to beginners.

Finally, one interesting way to invest in real estate, without buying a physical property outright, is to spend some of your money on shares in PropTech startups. PropTech, or Property Technology startups, are companies focused on developing tools and real estate designed to transform the property landscape.
